catalog_quote: only two tonemes on monosyllables are necessary: a high tone (transcribed ¹) and a low tone (transcribed ²). ... The tones are realized as falling on short vowel monosyllables, and level on long vowels. ... Tone is not contrastive for syllables with aspirated consonants. Such syllables normally have low tone when the vowel is long, and high tone when it is short. ... In dissyllabic words, when the first syllable is in the high tone, this tone spreads to the next syllable. For instance ɲeː¹ŋgɔ¹ ‘pillow’ <sngas.mgo> has high tone on the second syllable in spite of the fact that this syllable, when used in isolation, is in the low tone ŋgɔ² ‘head’ <mgo>. This rule of rightward tonal spread HL > HH occurs in also nominal compounds. It does not apply to the case markers and some verbal suffixes which are always realized low. audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the held HAL v2 PDF/text (sec. 2.3, printed pp. 6-8). (2) The deciding source is a specialist's full phonological profile (preprint of the 2014 Academia Sinica chapter that Glottolog ranks first for this languoid); no better or instrumental description of Cone prosody exists per Glottolog and web search. (3) Three open sources fetched sources now on another Cone dialect (Bragkhoglung: Suzuki 2012 p.3, Suzuki 2017 p.45, Zou & Suzuki 2022 pp.4-5) all describe a two-way word-tone (pitch) system with the contrast located at the word onset and say nothing of stress -- matching our 'tonal, H vs L contrastive on the first syllable, non-initial tones predictable' coding. (4) Only upgrade available is bibliographic: add the published Jacques 2014 citation alongside the preprint; no recode.

sources.citation: Zou, Yuxia & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2022. Five folktales of Bragkhoglung Tibetan of Cone. Himalayan Linguistics Archive 11: 1-85. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8h61w7r8
sources.quote: 'Bragkhoglung Tibetan is a language with distinctive tones.' ... '55 (high level short), 51 (falling short), 12 (low short), and 14 (low long) are attested for a monosyllabic word. For disyllabic combinations, another set of four pitch height patterns appears: 55-55, 11-55, 11-51, and 11-14'; fn. 10 cites Suzuki (2012): 'Suprasegmentals: word-tone system with two types, high and low.' No stress mentioned.

sources.citation: Suzuki, Hiroyuki. 2017. Suprasegmentals in Tibetic languages of the eastern Tibetosphere: from a geolinguistic perspective. Studies in Asian Geolinguistics VII (Tone and Accent): 41-49. ILCAA. https://publication.aa-ken.jp/
sources.quote: Typology of Eastern-Section Tibetic suprasegmentals lists Cone under '(D) pitch distinction': 'Type D, Cone (Qu 1962, rNam-rgyal Tshe-brten 2008, Suzuki 2012c)'; stress-type suprasegmentals (Type E / 'SA') are attributed to Amdo varieties, not to Cone.

sources.citation: Suzuki, Hiroyuki. 2012. Kanshuku-sho Kannan-shu Takuji-ken no Chibetto-go hogen ni tsuite: zobun taio keishiki kara mita Bragkhoglung hogen no hogen tokucho [On the Tibetan dialect of Cone County, Gannan, Gansu: dialectal features of the Bragkhoglung dialect seen from Written Tibetan correspondences]. Kyoto University Linguistic Research 31: 1-23. doi:10.14989/182195
sources.quote: (Japanese) 'Two tones are recognised, each bearing on the word as a unit: high word-onset vs low word-onset. Only the pitch of the word onset is distinctive; whether there is a fall toward syllable/word end is not distinctive, and polysyllabic words usually show a falling intonation.' Also notes (fn. 9, p. 12) that rNam-rgyal Tshe-brtan (2008) gives no consistent description of tone. No stress/accent described.
